label: Netlists as hypergraphs
lesson:
# Netlists as hypergraphs

A netlist is a set of cells joined by nets, and a net can join any number of cells. The natural mathematical object is therefore a hypergraph, not a graph: vertices are cells, hyperedges are nets. Partitioners, placers and routers all start from this representation, so a tool designer must know what it counts, what it hides, and how its basic statistics (pins, degrees, neighbourhoods) drive runtime and memory.

## Cells, nets and pins

A hypergraph $H = (V, E)$ has a vertex set $V$ and a family $E$ of hyperedges, each a subset of $V$ with at least two members. In a netlist, $V$ is the set of cells (or of pins, in a pin-level model) and each net $e \in E$ is the set of cells it touches. The incidence between a cell and a net is a **pin**. The total pin count $P = \sum_{e} |e|$ is the true size of a netlist: almost every algorithm in physical design runs in time proportional to $P$, not to the number of cells or nets.

For example, nets $n_1 = \{c_1, c_2, c_3\}$, $n_2 = \{c_2, c_4\}$ and $n_3 = \{c_1, c_3, c_4, c_5\}$ have sizes 3, 2 and 4, so $P = 9$ pins over 5 cells and 3 nets. Real designs average roughly three to four pins per net, but a few clock and reset nets have thousands.

## Degrees and neighbourhoods

The **degree** of a cell is the number of nets incident to it, and the size of a net is its own degree as a hyperedge. Two cells are **neighbours** if some net contains both. Neighbourhoods are what local algorithms touch: a Fiduccia-Mattheyses move updates the gains of the neighbours of the moved cell, and a placer's gradient for a cell depends on the nets it is on.

Take $n_1 = \{c_1, c_2, c_3\}$, $n_3 = \{c_1, c_3, c_4, c_5\}$. Cell $c_1$ has degree 2, and its neighbourhood is the union of its nets minus itself: $\{c_2, c_3, c_4, c_5\}$, four cells. Cell $c_3$ shares both nets with $c_1$ but is counted once. Summing all cell degrees gives $P$ again, which is the double-counting identity $\sum_v \deg(v) = \sum_e |e|$.

## What the hypergraph abstracts away

The hypergraph keeps connectivity and nothing else. It forgets which pin of a cell a net uses, which pin drives the net, cell sizes, and geometry. Partitioning needs only connectivity and cell area, so the plain hypergraph (with vertex weights) is its exact input. Timing needs direction, so it uses a directed pin graph instead. Placement needs pin offsets inside cells.

The abstraction has a real cost: converting a hyperedge to ordinary graph edges, as many algorithms want, distorts the objective, and a large net of $k$ pins becomes $k(k-1)/2$ edges if expanded naively. A tool designer chooses the representation to match what the algorithm must compute, and keeps hyperedges native where the objective (cut nets, net wirelength) is defined per net.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design: From Graph Partitioning to Timing Closure" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 1 and chapter 2; Karypis and Kumar's hMETIS manual for the hypergraph input format.

problems.q: A netlist has cells c1 to c6 and nets n1 = {c4, c6}; n2 = {c1, c3, c4}; n3 = {c4, c5}; n4 = {c2, c3, c4, c5}. Seen as a hypergraph, how many pins (vertex-hyperedge incidences) does it have?
problems.e: Each net contributes one pin per cell it touches. The net sizes are 2, 3, 2, 4, which sum to 11.

problems.e: Each net contributes one pin per cell it touches. The net sizes are 4, 4, 4, 4, 4, which sum to 20.

problems.e: Each net contributes one pin per cell it touches. The net sizes are 2, 4, 3, 3, 3, 3, which sum to 18.

problems.e: c3 appears on n2, n4, so its degree is 2.

problems.e: c3 appears on n1, n2, n4, so its degree is 3.

problems.e: c6 appears on n3, n6, so its degree is 2.

problems.q: A netlist has cells c1 to c5 and nets n1 = {c1, c2, c3}; n2 = {c1, c2, c4}; n3 = {c1, c2, c5}; n4 = {c4, c5}; n5 = {c2, c3, c4}. How many distinct other cells share at least one net with c5?
problems.e: Take the union of the nets on c5 and drop c5 itself: {c1, c2, c4}, which is 3 cells. A cell on two nets with the same neighbour counts that neighbour once.

problems.q: A netlist has cells c1 to c6 and nets n1 = {c1, c2, c3, c4}; n2 = {c1, c2, c4, c6}; n3 = {c3, c5}; n4 = {c2, c3, c4, c6}. How many distinct other cells share at least one net with c6?
problems.e: Take the union of the nets on c6 and drop c6 itself: {c1, c2, c3, c4}, which is 4 cells. A cell on two nets with the same neighbour counts that neighbour once.

problems.q: A netlist has cells c1 to c7 and nets n1 = {c2, c5, c6}; n2 = {c1, c4}; n3 = {c1, c7}; n4 = {c2, c4, c5}; n5 = {c4, c7}; n6 = {c3, c7}; n7 = {c1, c2, c5, c7}. How many distinct other cells share at least one net with c2?
problems.e: Take the union of the nets on c2 and drop c2 itself: {c1, c4, c5, c6, c7}, which is 5 cells. A cell on two nets with the same neighbour counts that neighbour once.

label: Directed pin graphs of drivers and sinks
lesson:
# Directed pin graphs of drivers and sinks

Timing analysis, levelization and loop detection need to know which way signals flow. A net has one driver pin and some sink pins, so the netlist becomes a directed graph with an arc from each driver to each of its sinks. This representation is the substrate of static timing, logic simulation and incremental analysis, and its in-degrees, out-degrees and reachable cones are the quantities those engines manipulate.

## From nets to driver-to-sink arcs

Each net $e$ with $k$ pins has exactly one driver (an output pin, or a primary input) and $k-1$ sinks (input pins, or primary outputs). The **pin graph** has a vertex per pin, or per cell when each cell has one output, and an arc from the driver to each sink. So a $k$-pin net contributes $k - 1$ arcs: this is the star model with the driver as centre and a direction attached.

Nets $n_1$ driven by $c_1$ with sinks $c_3, c_4$, and $n_2$ driven by $c_2$ with sink $c_4$ give arcs $c_1 \to c_3$, $c_1 \to c_4$, $c_2 \to c_4$: three arcs from nets of sizes 3 and 2. Inside a cell, timing tools add internal arcs from each input pin to each output pin it affects, which is how a cell-level graph becomes a pin-level timing graph.

## Fan-in, fanout and cones

The out-degree of a driver is its **fanout**, the number of sinks it must charge. The in-degree of a cell is its **fan-in**, the number of its inputs that are driven. The **transitive fanout cone** of a vertex is everything reachable from it along arcs; the transitive fan-in cone is everything that reaches it.

Cones bound the effect of a change: if a cell's delay changes, only arrival times in its fanout cone can change, and only required times in its fan-in cone. For arcs $c_2 \to c_3$, $c_2 \to c_6$, $c_3 \to c_8$, the fanout cone of $c_2$ is $\{c_3, c_6, c_8\}$: three cells, found by depth-first search in time linear in the arcs visited. Logic synthesis uses fan-in cones the same way, as the region a rewrite of one output can touch.

## Direction as a source of structure

Undirected models cannot express that a signal flows one way. The directed pin graph of a combinational netlist is acyclic, which is what lets timers and simulators process vertices in topological order. Sequential elements break the cycles: a timer cuts the graph at flip-flop data pins and starts new paths at their clock-to-output arcs.

Direction also changes the net models a tool should use. A partitioner treats all pins of a net symmetrically, but a timing-driven placer weights the driver-to-critical-sink connections more than others. And a bidirectional pin, or a tristate bus with several drivers, does not fit the one-driver assumption; tools either model it specially or report it, which is one reason designs avoid internal tristates.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design: From Graph Partitioning to Timing Closure" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 8 on timing graphs; the OpenSTA documentation on its timing graph.

Build the directed pin graph with one arc from each net's driver to each of its sinks. What is the in-degree of c8, the number of its input pins that are driven?

label: Clique and star models of a net
lesson:
# Clique and star models of a net

Many algorithms, from spectral partitioning to quadratic placement, need an ordinary weighted graph rather than a hypergraph. The two standard ways to turn a $k$-pin net into edges are the clique model (an edge between every pair of pins) and the star model (a new centre vertex joined to every pin). The choice changes the edge count, the memory footprint and the weights the objective sees, so it is a design decision with consequences.

## Clique and star expansions

The **clique model** replaces a $k$-pin net by the complete graph $K_k$ on its pins, with $\binom{k}{2} = k(k-1)/2$ edges. The **star model** adds one auxiliary vertex for the net and joins it to each pin, giving $k$ edges and one extra vertex. Two-pin nets are a single edge in either model.

Edge counts matter because nets are skewed. A netlist with nets of sizes 3, 2 and 8 has $3 + 1 + 28 = 32$ clique edges, and the one 8-pin net accounts for 28 of them. A 1,000-pin enable net would add almost 500,000 clique edges on its own, against 1,000 star edges. This is why tools use stars for large nets, or drop nets above a size threshold from connectivity-driven steps.

## Weighting clique edges

Expanding every net into a unit-weight clique overweights large nets: a 10-pin net contributes 45 edges and would dominate a 2-pin net's single edge. So clique edges are weighted by net size. Two common choices are $w = 1/(k-1)$, which makes the total weight of a $k$-pin net $k/2$, and $w = 2/k$, which makes it $k-1$, the number of edges of a spanning tree.

When several nets contain the same pair of cells, their edges are merged by adding weights. For cells $c_1, c_4$ on a 5-pin net, a 3-pin net and another 3-pin net, the merged weight under $1/(k-1)$ is $1/4 + 1/2 + 1/2 = 1.25$. This merged weight is what a spectral partitioner or a quadratic placer actually sees between those two cells.

## Choosing a model

The star model is equivalent to the clique for quadratic objectives when the star centre is a free vertex at the optimum: eliminating the centre from a star with edge weights $w$ gives a clique with weights $w/k$ on its pins. That equivalence is why quadratic placers can use stars for large nets without changing the solution, while saving memory and solver time.

For cut-based objectives no graph model is exact. A clique charges a split net more when its pins are split evenly than when one pin is split off, while the hypergraph charges 1 either way. Hybrid schemes are common: cliques for small nets, stars above a threshold of a few pins, and the hybrid Bound2Bound model in analytical placers, which connects each pin to the net's two extreme pins and reproduces half-perimeter wirelength exactly at the current placement.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design: From Graph Partitioning to Timing Closure" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 4; Spindler, Schlichtmann and Johannes, "Kraftwerk2" (IEEE TCAD, 2008) for the Bound2Bound model.

Each net of k pins is expanded as a clique whose edges get weight $1/(k-1)$, and parallel edges are merged by adding weights. What is the weight of the merged edge between c7 and c4? Round to 2 decimal places.

label: Compressed incidence storage for netlists
prereqs: The product and sum rules for counting
lesson:
# Compressed incidence storage for netlists

A million-cell netlist has several million pins, and every pass of a partitioner or placer walks them. The data structure that holds incidence decides cache behaviour, memory use and the cost of each traversal. Engines almost universally store a netlist in compressed sparse form, an offset array plus an index array in each direction, so a tool designer must be able to compute offsets and sizes and know why this layout wins.

## Offsets and pin arrays

Compressed storage of net-to-pin incidence uses two arrays. The pin array lists the cells of net 0, then net 1, and so on, back to back. The offset array netStart has length $m + 1$ for $m$ nets: netStart[j] is where net $j$'s pins begin, and netStart[m] equals the total pin count $P$. Net $j$'s pins are pin[netStart[j]] through pin[netStart[j+1] - 1], and its size is the difference of consecutive offsets.

With nets of sizes 2, 4, 4 and 2, the offsets are 0, 2, 6, 10, 12. Net 2 (the third) starts at index 6 and has $10 - 6 = 4$ pins. Each offset is a prefix sum of net sizes, so the array is built in one pass after counting.

## The transpose: cell-to-net incidence

Algorithms need both directions. An FM move starts from a cell and must reach its nets, then from each net reach its other cells. So engines also store cell-to-net incidence: an offset array cellStart of length $n + 1$ for $n$ cells and an index array of net ids. cellStart[c] is the sum of the degrees of the cells before $c$.

Building the transpose is a counting sort: count each cell's degree in one pass over the pins, take prefix sums to get cellStart, then make a second pass that drops each net id into its cell's slot. If degrees are 2, 2, 2, 4, 1, then cellStart is 0, 2, 4, 6, 10, 11. Both directions together are what make one FM pass linear in $P$.

## Why compressed storage wins

Storing both directions takes $(m + 1) + P + (n + 1) + P$ integers, about $2P$ for large designs. With 4-byte integers, 6 cells, 6 nets and 17 pins need $4 \times (7 + 17 + 7 + 17) = 192$ bytes. A pointer-based structure (a list object per net and per cell) costs several times more and scatters data across memory.

The contiguous layout means a traversal of a net's pins is a sequential read, which caches and prefetches well and vectorizes. The price is that the structure is static: inserting a pin means shifting arrays. Engines therefore build the compressed form once per run, or once per level in a multilevel partitioner, and handle incremental netlist edits (ECOs, buffer insertion) with a separate dynamic structure or a periodic rebuild.

## Going deeper

Saad, "Iterative Methods for Sparse Linear Systems" (2nd ed., 2003), chapter 3, for the compressed sparse row format; the KaHyPar and hMETIS source code for hypergraph storage.

problems.q: Nets: n1 = {c1, c2, c7}; n2 = {c1, c7}; n3 = {c3, c4}; n4 = {c2, c7}; n5 = {c1, c4, c5, c6}. The tool stores net-to-pin incidence in compressed form: an offset array netStart of length m + 1 and a pin array listing each net's cells in order, so net j's pins are pin[netStart[j]] up to pin[netStart[j+1] - 1], with nets indexed from 0 (n1 is index 0). label: Pre-order and post-order traversal of a rooted tree
lesson:
# Pre-order and post-order traversal of a rooted tree

Routed nets, clock trees, Steiner trees and buffer trees are rooted trees: a driver at the root, sinks at the leaves. Almost every computation on them is a traversal. Post-order (children before parent) accumulates quantities that flow upward, such as downstream capacitance; pre-order (parent before children) pushes quantities downward, such as delay from the root. Elmore delay, van Ginneken buffering and clock skew analysis are all built from these two passes.

## Pre-order: parent before children

In a rooted tree every node except the root has one parent. A **pre-order** traversal visits a node, then recursively visits each child subtree in a fixed child order. The root comes first, and each node appears before all of its descendants.

Take root 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 with children 4 and 5, and node 4 with children 6 and 7, visiting children in increasing label order. Pre-order is 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 5, 3: from 2 we finish its whole subtree (4, 6, 7, then 5) before reaching 3. The sixth node visited is 5. Pre-order is the right order whenever a node's value depends on its parent's, because the parent is always finished first.

## Post-order: children before parent

A **post-order** traversal recursively visits every child subtree first and visits the node last. Leaves come first, the root last, and every node appears after all of its descendants.

For the same tree, post-order is 6, 7, 4, 5, 2, 3, 1. Node 4 waits for 6 and 7, node 2 waits for 4 and 5, and the root waits for everything. The fourth node visited is 5. Post-order is the right order whenever a node's value is a combination of its children's values, because those values are ready when the node is reached. Both traversals take time linear in the number of nodes, and an explicit stack replaces recursion for trees deep enough to overflow the call stack.

## Two passes on an RC tree

Elmore delay on an RC tree uses both passes. A post-order pass computes the downstream capacitance $C_{down}(v) = C_v + \sum_{c \in \text{children}(v)} C_{down}(c)$. A pre-order pass then computes delay $T(v) = T(\text{parent}(v)) + R_{edge(v)}\,C_{down}(v)$.

With capacitances $C_2 = 9$, $C_4 = 8$ and $C_6 = 3$ fF, where 4 and 6 are the children of 2 and both are leaves, $C_{down}(2) = 9 + 8 + 3 = 20$ fF. The same pattern appears in van Ginneken's buffer insertion (candidate solutions merge bottom-up, then the chosen buffers are placed top-down) and in clock-tree synthesis (subtree delays merge bottom-up, then the tree is embedded top-down). Recognizing which quantity flows which way is the design step.

## Going deeper

Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, "Introduction to Algorithms" (4th ed., 2022), chapter 12; Rubinstein, Penfield and Horowitz, "Signal delay in RC tree networks" (IEEE TCAD, 1983).

label: Topological sorting of a DAG
prereqs: Directed pin graphs of drivers and sinks
lesson:
# Topological sorting of a DAG

A combinational netlist, cut at its registers, is a directed acyclic graph. A topological order lists its vertices so that every arc goes forward, which is exactly the order in which arrival times, logic values or signal probabilities can be computed in one pass. Timers, simulators and synthesis tools all start by sorting the graph, and they must do it in linear time and update it as the netlist changes.

## Kahn's algorithm

Kahn's algorithm keeps the in-degree of every vertex. Vertices with in-degree 0 (the primary inputs and register outputs) are ready. Repeatedly remove a ready vertex, append it to the order, and decrement the in-degree of each of its successors; any successor that reaches 0 becomes ready. If vertices remain when no vertex is ready, the graph has a cycle.

With arcs $v_1 \to v_2$, $v_1 \to v_5$, $v_2 \to v_3$, $v_4 \to v_3$, $v_5 \to v_3$ and the smallest-label ready vertex removed first, the ready set starts as $\{v_1, v_4\}$. The order is $v_1, v_2, v_4, v_5, v_3$. Each arc is touched once, so the cost is $O(V + E)$.

## Depth-first search order

The second standard method runs depth-first search and records each vertex when it finishes (all its descendants are done). Reversing the finishing order gives a topological order, because in a DAG a vertex always finishes after everything reachable from it. A back arc found during the search, an arc to a vertex still on the recursion stack, proves a cycle.

Both methods are linear. Kahn's algorithm is natural for levelized processing and for parallel evaluation, since every vertex in the ready set can be processed at once. The DFS method is natural when the tool already traverses cones, for example when it sorts only the fan-in cone of one output. Real timers keep a level for every vertex, computed with Kahn's algorithm, and sort dirty vertices by level during incremental updates.

## How free the order is

A DAG usually has many topological orders. The constraints come only from ancestors and descendants: a vertex must follow all of its ancestors and precede all of its descendants. So the earliest position a vertex $v$ can take is $|\text{anc}(v)| + 1$, and the latest is $n - |\text{desc}(v)|$. Everything else is free.

That freedom is useful. Simulators choose orders that keep related vertices close in memory; parallel timers choose orders that expose independent vertices; synthesis tools choose orders that make cut enumeration cache-friendly. It also means a tool must not depend on one particular order for correctness, only on the order being topological, which is a property a differential test can check directly.

## Going deeper

Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, "Introduction to Algorithms" (4th ed., 2022), section 20.4; Kahn, "Topological sorting of large networks" (CACM, 1962).

label: Levelization of a combinational netlist
prereqs: Directed pin graphs of drivers and sinks
lesson:
# Levelization of a combinational netlist

Levelization assigns each vertex of a combinational DAG a level: primary inputs and register outputs at level 0, and every other vertex one above its deepest fanin. Levels give a ready-made schedule for evaluation, a measure of logic depth, and the bucket key that incremental timers use to process dirty vertices in order. It is one of the first passes every simulator and timer runs.

## Levels from fanins

Define $\ell(v) = 0$ for a vertex with no incoming arcs, and $\ell(v) = 1 + \max_{u \to v} \ell(u)$ otherwise. This is the longest path, counted in arcs, from any source to $v$. It is computed in one pass over a topological order.

With arcs $v_1 \to v_4$, $v_2 \to v_4$, $v_4 \to v_5$, $v_4 \to v_6$, $v_3 \to v_6$, $v_5 \to v_7$: $v_1, v_2, v_3$ are at level 0, $v_4$ at level 1, $v_5$ and $v_6$ at level 2 (since $v_6$'s deepest fanin $v_4$ is at level 1), and $v_7$ at level 3. Every arc goes from a lower level to a strictly higher one, so the levels themselves are a valid evaluation schedule.

## Depth and width

The number of levels is the **logic depth** plus one, counting level 0. Depth correlates with delay and is what synthesis minimizes when it optimizes for speed before timing information is available. The number of vertices at a level is the **width** of that level, the parallelism available to a levelized simulator or a parallel timer that processes one level at a time.

In the example, the levels hold $\{v_1, v_2, v_3\}$, $\{v_4\}$, $\{v_5, v_6\}$ and $\{v_7\}$: four levels, widths 3, 1, 2, 1. A narrow level is a synchronization bottleneck for parallel evaluation. A long tail of narrow levels usually means a deep carry chain or a long serial path, which synthesis may restructure.

## Levels in incremental analysis

After an edit, an incremental timer must recompute arrival times only for dirty vertices, and it must process them in topological order. Keeping a level for every vertex makes this cheap: dirty vertices go into a priority queue or a bucket array keyed by level, and the timer pops them lowest level first. A vertex is then never recomputed before its fanins.

Edits can change levels. Inserting a buffer on an arc raises the level of everything downstream of that arc by up to one; deleting a gate can lower levels. Timers either propagate level changes eagerly or tolerate stale levels that remain topologically consistent, since correctness only needs every arc to point to a higher level, not the exact longest-path value. This distinction, an exact invariant versus a sufficient one, recurs throughout incremental engine design.

## Going deeper

Abramovici, Breuer and Friedman, "Digital Systems Testing and Testable Design" (1990), the chapter on logic simulation; Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design: From Graph Partitioning to Timing Closure" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 8.

label: Strongly connected components and combinational loops
prereqs: Directed pin graphs of drivers and sinks
lesson:
# Strongly connected components and combinational loops

A combinational loop, a cycle that passes through no register, breaks static timing, makes simulation oscillate or depend on order, and is almost always a design error. Finding loops is a strongly-connected-components problem: every vertex on a cycle lies in a component with at least two vertices. Lint tools, synthesis front ends and timers all run this check, and they must report the loop in a form a designer can act on.

## Components by mutual reachability

Two vertices of a directed graph are strongly connected if each can reach the other. This is an equivalence relation, and its classes are the **strongly connected components**. A vertex on no cycle is a component by itself. Contracting each component to a single vertex gives the condensation, which is always a DAG.

Arcs $v_1 \to v_2$, $v_2 \to v_1$, $v_1 \to v_6$, $v_6 \to v_3$, $v_6 \to v_4$, $v_4 \to v_3$, $v_6 \to v_5$, $v_7 \to v_2$ give components $\{v_1, v_2\}$, $\{v_3\}$, $\{v_4\}$, $\{v_5\}$, $\{v_6\}$, $\{v_7\}$: six components, one of them a 2-cycle. The condensation is acyclic, so a timer could still levelize everything except the loop.

## Linear-time algorithms

Tarjan's algorithm finds all components in one depth-first search. It gives each vertex a discovery index and a lowlink, the smallest index reachable from its subtree through at most one back arc, and keeps visited vertices on a stack. When a vertex's lowlink equals its own index, it is the root of a component, and the component is popped from the stack.

Kosaraju's algorithm uses two searches: one on the graph to get finishing times, then one on the reversed graph in decreasing finishing time, where each search tree is a component. Both run in $O(V + E)$. On a netlist with millions of pins this is a fraction of a second, which is why loop checks run on every read of a design.

## From components to loop reports

Every vertex in a component of size two or more lies on a cycle, given no self-loops. So the number of vertices to flag is the total size of all nontrivial components. A self-loop, an output fed directly to its own input, makes a single vertex a loop and must be checked separately.

A component is not yet a useful report: it may hold hundreds of gates. Tools extract one short cycle inside it (a breadth-first search from one member back to itself) and report that path. To proceed with timing anyway, a timer breaks loops by disabling chosen arcs, which is a feedback arc set problem; minimum feedback arc set is NP-hard, so timers break arcs heuristically and warn. Some loops are intentional, such as latch-based or asynchronous structures, and designers mark them so the tool does not break them blindly.

## Going deeper

Tarjan, "Depth-first search and linear graph algorithms" (SIAM J. Computing, 1972); the OpenSTA documentation on combinational loops.

label: Longest paths in a DAG
lesson:
# Longest paths in a DAG

Static timing analysis is, at its core, a longest-path computation on a DAG: the latest arrival time at a vertex is the longest path, by delay, from any timing start point. Longest paths are NP-hard in general graphs but linear on DAGs, which is the single most important fact behind block-based timing. The same recurrence gives logic depth, schedule length in high-level synthesis and positions in layout compaction.

## The max-plus recurrence

Give each arc $u \to v$ a delay $d(u,v)$ and each source an arrival time $a(s)$. For every other vertex,

$$a(v) = \max_{u \to v} \big(a(u) + d(u,v)\big).$$

The recurrence is well defined only because the graph is acyclic: process vertices in topological order and every $a(u)$ is final before it is used. Arcs $v_1 \to v_3$ (4), $v_3 \to v_4$ (3), $v_2 \to v_4$ (9), $v_3 \to v_5$ (5), $v_4 \to v_5$ (9) with $a(v_1) = a(v_2) = 0$ give $a(v_3) = 4$, $a(v_4) = \max(4+3, 0+9) = 9$, $a(v_5) = \max(4+5, 9+9) = 18$.

## Why acyclicity makes it easy

On a general graph, the longest simple path is NP-hard: it contains the Hamiltonian path problem. On a DAG every path is simple, and the recurrence above solves the problem in $O(V + E)$ by dynamic programming. Equivalently, negate every delay and run a shortest-path computation; on a DAG no negative cycle can exist.

Nonzero input arrivals simply initialize the sources. If inputs arrive at $v_1$ at 5 ps and $v_2$ at 0 ps, every path from $v_1$ gains 5 ps, and the maximum at each vertex is taken over these offset paths. Real timers carry separate rise and fall arrivals and propagate slews alongside, but the structure stays the same max-plus pass in topological order.

## Paths versus blocks

The recurrence keeps one number per vertex, the latest arrival, rather than every path. That is **block-based** analysis: linear time, but it loses which path produced the maximum unless a back-pointer is stored. **Path-based** analysis enumerates paths, which can be exponentially many, but can apply path-specific effects such as removing common clock pessimism or computing exact path delay with a better model.

Production timers do both: a block-based pass finds arrivals and slacks everywhere, then path enumeration extracts the worst few paths per endpoint for reporting and refinement. The max operator is also the reason timing is pessimistic under variation: the maximum of random arrivals is not Gaussian, which statistical timers must approximate.

## Going deeper

label: Reverse-topological passes and node slack
prereqs: Pre-order and post-order traversal of a rooted tree
lesson:
# Reverse-topological passes and node slack

A forward pass computes the latest arrival at every vertex. A backward pass, in reverse topological order, computes the latest time each vertex may settle without violating any endpoint requirement. Their difference is slack, the per-vertex margin that drives every timing optimizer. As a graph algorithm the backward pass is the min-plus mirror of the forward pass, and together they identify the critical subgraph.

## Required times flow backward

Give every endpoint a required time $q(s)$. For every other vertex,

$$q(v) = \min_{v \to w} \big(q(w) - d(v,w)\big),$$

computed in reverse topological order so that every successor is final. The minimum appears because the vertex must satisfy its tightest successor.

With arcs $v_1 \to v_4$ (1), $v_2 \to v_3$ (5), $v_2 \to v_4$ (5), $v_3 \to v_5$ (9), $v_4 \to v_5$ (7) and endpoint $v_5$ required at 34 ps: $q(v_3) = 25$, $q(v_4) = 27$, $q(v_2) = \min(25 - 5, 27 - 5) = 20$, $q(v_1) = 26$. The pass costs $O(V + E)$, the same as the forward pass, and it uses the same topological order read backward.

## Slack at a vertex

The slack of a vertex is $s(v) = q(v) - a(v)$: how much later the signal at $v$ could settle before some endpoint fails. Negative slack means at least one path through $v$ violates its requirement. In the example, arrivals are $a(v_1) = 0$, $a(v_4) = 5$, so $s(v_1) = 26$ and $s(v_4) = 22$.

Slack is a path property stored on vertices: $s(v)$ equals the slack of the worst endpoint path through $v$. So an optimizer reading a vertex's slack knows the worst case through that vertex without enumerating paths. Arc slack, $q(w) - a(v) - d(v,w)$, is the analogous quantity for an arc and tells a sizer which fanin of a gate is the critical one.

## The critical subgraph

When the required time is set to the latest endpoint arrival, the worst slack in the graph is zero, and the vertices with zero slack are exactly those on at least one longest path. They form the **critical subgraph**. Its size tells an optimizer how concentrated the problem is: one thin path can be fixed by sizing a few gates, while a wide critical region needs restructuring.

Both passes are linear, so a timer can recompute all slacks after each optimization step. The same pair of passes computes ASAP and ALAP times in high-level synthesis scheduling, where the difference is an operation's mobility, and early and late times in project scheduling. In every case, zero-slack vertices are the ones that cannot move without lengthening the whole schedule.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design: From Graph Partitioning to Timing Closure" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 8; De Micheli, "Synthesis and Optimization of Digital Circuits" (1994), chapter 5 on ASAP and ALAP scheduling.

label: Counting paths through a node
prereqs: The product and sum rules for counting
lesson:
# Counting paths through a node

The number of input-to-output paths in a netlist can be exponential in its size, which is why timers cannot enumerate paths and why path-based fault models and path coverage metrics need care. Counting paths is itself easy on a DAG, with the same dynamic program as longest paths but with sums in place of maxima. Path counts through a vertex also measure how much a single gate matters.

## Counting paths by dynamic programming

Let $N(v)$ be the number of paths from any source to $v$. Set $N(s) = 1$ at each source and $N(v) = \sum_{u \to v} N(u)$ otherwise, in topological order. The total number of source-to-sink paths is $\sum_{\text{sinks } t} N(t)$.

With sources $v_1, v_2$ and arcs $v_1 \to v_4$, $v_2 \to v_3$, $v_2 \to v_4$, $v_2 \to v_6$, $v_3 \to v_5$, $v_4 \to v_5$: $N(v_3) = 1$, $N(v_4) = 2$, $N(v_5) = 1 + 2 = 3$, $N(v_6) = 1$. The sinks are $v_5$ and $v_6$, so there are $3 + 1 = 4$ paths. The pass is linear, though the counts themselves can need many bits.

## Paths through one vertex

Run the same recurrence backward: $M(v) = \sum_{v \to w} M(w)$ with $M(t) = 1$ at sinks counts paths from $v$ to any sink. Every path into $v$ combines with every path out of it, so the number of source-to-sink paths through $v$ is $N(v) \cdot M(v)$.

If three paths reach a gate and four leave it, twelve paths pass through it. Path-based test generation, path delay fault coverage and criticality metrics all use these counts. A vertex with a huge product is a convergence point where many paths share hardware, so it is a natural target when an optimizer wants to improve many paths at once.

## Exponential path explosion

Reconvergent fanout multiplies paths. A chain of $k$ stages, each fanning out into $w_i$ parallel gates that reconverge, has $\prod_i w_i$ paths but only about $1 + \sum_i (w_i + 1)$ vertices. Ten stages of width 4 give $4^{10} \approx 10^6$ paths through about 50 vertices. Real datapaths, such as multipliers, are far worse.

This is the decisive argument for block-based timing: a per-vertex pass costs $O(V + E)$ while path enumeration costs time proportional to the number of paths. It is also why path-delay fault testing targets only selected paths, and why reports list the worst $k$ paths per endpoint using a best-first search over the DAG rather than all of them.

## Going deeper

Bushnell and Agrawal, "Essentials of Electronic Testing" (2000), chapter on path delay faults; Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design: From Graph Partitioning to Timing Closure" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 8.

label: Incremental updates on a DAG
lesson:
# Incremental updates on a DAG

Optimization loops change one gate, one wire or one buffer at a time and need updated timing after each change. Recomputing every arrival from scratch is linear in the design but far too slow when repeated a million times. Incremental algorithms recompute only the region a change can affect, and stop early where the change is absorbed. Designing that bookkeeping correctly is one of the central engineering problems of timers.

## The fanout cone bounds the work

If the delay of arc $u \to v$ changes, only arrivals at vertices reachable from $v$ can change, including $v$ itself. That set is the fanout cone of $v$, and an incremental timer marks it dirty. Required times change only in the fan-in cone of the changed arc's tail, $u$.

In a graph with arcs $v_1 \to v_3$, $v_3 \to v_4$, $v_3 \to v_7$, $v_4 \to v_7$, $v_1 \to v_5$, a change on $v_1 \to v_3$ marks $\{v_3, v_4, v_7\}$: three vertices, while $v_5$ is untouched. For a change near the outputs the cone is tiny; for a change near the inputs it can be most of the design. Timers keep the dirty set in a level-keyed queue so each vertex is recomputed after its fanins.

## Stopping early

Not every vertex in the cone actually changes. If arc $v_2 \to v_5$ slows by 5 ps but $v_5$'s arrival is set by another fanin with more margin than that, $a(v_5)$ is unchanged, and nothing downstream of $v_5$ needs recomputation through that route. An incremental timer recomputes a dirty vertex, compares the new arrival with the old, and propagates dirtiness to its successors only if the value changed.

So the work is proportional to the vertices whose values change plus their immediate fanouts, which is often far smaller than the cone. The test must be exact (or a tolerance that the signoff flow accepts), because skipping a vertex whose value changed by a tiny amount leaves stale values that later comparisons trust.

## Correctness of incremental results

An incremental engine is correct only if its results equal a full recomputation. That makes full recomputation the natural differential test: after a random sequence of edits, rerun the whole graph and compare every arrival and required time. Typical bugs are a missed dirty mark (an edit path that forgets to notify), stale levels after structural edits, and early stopping on a value that changed in a field not compared, such as slew.

Structural edits are harder than delay edits: inserting a buffer adds vertices and arcs, so levels and topological positions must be updated before propagation. Many timers handle structural edits by repairing levels locally and then running the same dirty-cone propagation. The speed of this loop is what makes timing-driven placement, sizing and ECO flows practical.

## Going deeper

The OpenSTA and OpenTimer documentation on incremental timing; Huang, Guo, Lin and Wong, "OpenTimer v2" (IEEE TCAD, 2021).

label: Routing grids as graphs
prereqs: The product and sum rules for counting
lesson:
# Routing grids as graphs

A router does not search the plane; it searches a graph. Global routers use a coarse grid of routing bins, and detailed routers use a fine grid of tracks on each metal layer, with vias between layers. Every routing algorithm's cost is set by the size of that graph, so a router designer must be able to count its vertices and edges and know what each modeling choice, preferred directions in particular, does to them.

## Vertices of a layered grid

A detailed-routing grid places a vertex at every intersection of a horizontal and a vertical track, on every metal layer. With $W$ columns, $H$ rows and $L$ layers there are $W \cdot H \cdot L$ vertices. A global-routing grid is the same structure at coarser granularity, where each vertex is a bin (a g-cell) holding many tracks, and edges carry capacities equal to the number of tracks crossing the bin boundary.

A block with 7 columns, 21 rows and 6 layers has $7 \times 21 \times 6 = 882$ vertices; a real detailed grid has billions, which is why detailed routers work in windows and global routers coarsen first. Vertices that fall on blockages or pins of other nets are removed or given infinite cost.

## Preferred directions and wire edges

Each metal layer has a **preferred direction**, alternating between horizontal and vertical from one layer to the next. Wire edges on a layer join neighbouring vertices only along its preferred direction: a horizontal layer has $(W - 1) H$ wire edges and a vertical layer $W (H - 1)$. Wrong-way wiring is either forbidden or heavily penalized.

With $W = 21$, $H = 6$ and three layers (horizontal, vertical, horizontal), the two horizontal layers contribute $2 \times 20 \times 6 = 240$ edges and the vertical layer $21 \times 5 = 105$, for 345 wire edges. Preferred directions halve the wire edges compared with a full grid on every layer, and they make the layers' wires parallel, which simplifies design-rule checking and keeps coupling predictable.

## Vias and edge costs

Via edges connect the same $(x, y)$ point on adjacent layers, so there are $W H (L - 1)$ of them. For a grid with 10 columns, 9 rows and three layers, the two horizontal layers give $2 \times 9 \times 9 = 162$ wire edges, the vertical layer gives $10 \times 8 = 80$, and vias add $10 \times 9 \times 2 = 180$, for 422 edges in total.

The router's real model sits in the edge costs: wirelength per unit, a larger cost per via (vias add resistance and hurt yield), congestion penalties on edges near capacity, and history costs in negotiated routing. Changing costs changes the routes without changing the graph. The graph's size, about $3 W H L$ edges, is what a maze search must explore, which motivates the bounded windows and A* guidance that real routers use.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design: From Graph Partitioning to Timing Closure" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 5; the TritonRoute and FastRoute documentation in OpenROAD.

label: Breadth-first wavefront search on a grid
lesson:
# Breadth-first wavefront search on a grid

Lee's maze-routing algorithm, from 1961, is breadth-first search on a grid graph: a wavefront expands from the source one step at a time, labelling each cell with its distance, until it reaches the target. It always finds a shortest path if one exists. Every later router, from line-probe methods to A*-guided detailed routers, is measured against it, and its wavefront picture is the clearest way to see what a search spends its time on.

## Wavefront labels

Label the source 0. At step $k$, every unlabelled, unblocked neighbour of a cell labelled $k$ receives label $k + 1$. With unit edge costs this is breadth-first search, and a cell's label is its shortest-path distance from the source around the blockages.

On an open grid a cell's label equals its Manhattan distance from the source. Blockages bend the wavefront: a wall of blocked cells with a single gap forces every label beyond the wall to be counted through the gap. A cell at Manhattan distance 3 behind such a wall might receive label 5 or more. Each cell is labelled once and examined once, so the search costs time linear in the number of cells reached.

## Reaching the target and retracing

The expansion stops when the target receives a label; that label is the length of a shortest route. The route is recovered by **retrace**: from the target, step to any neighbour whose label is one less, until the source is reached. When several neighbours qualify, routers prefer the one that continues in the current direction, which minimizes bends and therefore vias.

If the wavefront dies out before reaching the target, no route exists with the current blockages, and the router must rip up other nets to make room. The difference between the label at the target and the Manhattan distance is the detour the blockages force, a quantity routers watch because long detours waste tracks and add delay.

## The cost of the wavefront

The number of cells at label exactly $k$ is the size of wavefront $k$. On an open grid it grows linearly with $k$ (up to $4k$ cells), so reaching a target at distance $D$ explores about $2D^2$ cells: quadratic in the route length, in every direction, including directions away from the target.

That waste is why practical routers bound the search to a box around the source and target, use bidirectional search, or guide it with A*. Lee's algorithm also handles only unit costs; non-uniform costs (vias, congestion, preferred direction) need Dijkstra's algorithm, of which Lee's search is the unit-cost special case. Its memory cost, one label per cell, motivated the compact coding schemes of early routers.

## Going deeper

Lee, "An algorithm for path connections and its applications" (IRE Trans. Electronic Computers, 1961); Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design: From Graph Partitioning to Timing Closure" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 5.

label: Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm
prereqs: Breadth-first wavefront search on a grid
lesson:
# Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm

Real routing costs are not uniform: vias cost more than wire, congested edges cost more than free ones, and wrong-way segments are penalized. Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths with any non-negative edge costs, and it is the engine inside maze routers, global routers and many timing-driven tools. Knowing exactly what it settles, when, and at what cost per operation is basic equipment for a router designer.

## Settling vertices in order of distance

Dijkstra's algorithm keeps a tentative distance $d(v)$ for every vertex, starting with $d(s) = 0$ and $\infty$ elsewhere. It repeatedly **settles** the unsettled vertex with the smallest tentative distance, then relaxes its edges: for each neighbour $w$, set $d(w) = \min(d(w), d(v) + c(v,w))$.

Because costs are non-negative, a settled vertex's distance is final: any other route to it would pass through an unsettled vertex whose distance is already at least as large. With edges $v_1$-$v_4$ (2), $v_1$-$v_3$ (5), $v_4$-$v_6$ (3), $v_4$-$v_5$ (4), $v_2$-$v_6$ (4), the settling order from $v_1$ is $v_1$ (0), $v_4$ (2), then $v_3$ (5) and $v_6$ (5), then $v_5$ (6), then $v_2$ (9).

## Tentative distances during the run

Between settles, tentative distances are upper bounds that only decrease. After the source is settled, each neighbour's tentative distance is its direct edge cost; later settles may lower it. A vertex $v_6$ that first gets $d = 8$ through a direct edge may drop to 8 or lower when a cheaper two-edge route through $v_5$ is found.

The order of settling is fixed by the distances, with ties broken by a rule such as smaller label. A router's behaviour depends on that rule: when many equal-cost routes exist, the tie-break decides which one is found, which is why routers add small biases (prefer the current direction, prefer lower layers) rather than leaving ties to chance.

## Data structures and limits

With a binary heap, Dijkstra runs in $O((V + E)\log V)$; with a Fibonacci heap, $O(E + V \log V)$. On grid graphs with small integer costs, a bucket queue indexed by distance gives near-linear time, which many routers use. Each settle pops the heap, and each successful relaxation is a decrease-key or a lazy reinsert.

Two limits matter. Negative edge costs break the settled-is-final argument, so problems with negative costs need Bellman-Ford. And Dijkstra explores every direction equally: on a grid it settles a diamond of vertices around the source until the target is reached, which wastes work. A* fixes that by adding a heuristic to the priority, without giving up optimality when the heuristic is admissible.

## Going deeper

Dijkstra, "A note on two problems in connexion with graphs" (Numerische Mathematik, 1959); Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, "Introduction to Algorithms" (4th ed., 2022), section 22.3.

label: Bellman-Ford and negative edge weights
lesson:
# Bellman-Ford and negative edge weights

Some EDA graphs carry negative weights: constraint graphs for layout compaction and retiming, timing graphs with hold constraints written as negative arcs, and residual graphs in min-cost flow. Dijkstra's algorithm fails on them, and a negative cycle means the problem has no solution at all. Bellman-Ford handles negative weights, detects negative cycles, and is the workhorse for difference constraints.

## Relaxing every arc in rounds

Bellman-Ford sets $d(s) = 0$ and $d(v) = \infty$ elsewhere, then performs rounds. In each round it relaxes every arc once: $d(v) = \min(d(v), d(u) + w(u,v))$. After round $k$, $d(v)$ is at most the length of the shortest path from $s$ to $v$ that uses at most $k$ arcs. A shortest simple path has at most $n - 1$ arcs, so $n - 1$ rounds suffice when there is no negative cycle.

Arcs $v_1 \to v_3$ (3), $v_3 \to v_5$ (2), $v_2 \to v_6$ (-4), $v_1 \to v_2$ (8) give $d(v_6) = 8 - 4 = 4$, found once $v_2$ has its distance. The algorithm costs $O(VE)$, slower than Dijkstra, but it never assumes that a vertex's distance is final early.

## Arc order and early termination

The round bound is a worst case. Within a round, a relaxation can use a value lowered earlier in the same round, so the arc order matters: if arcs happen to be listed in topological order, one round finishes the job; if they are listed in reverse, each round advances distances by only one arc. After round 1 an estimate may still be too high, and later rounds lower it.

So implementations stop as soon as a full round changes nothing, and they keep a queue of vertices whose distance changed so that only their outgoing arcs are relaxed next (the queue-based variant, often called SPFA). On sparse, nearly acyclic constraint graphs this makes Bellman-Ford fast in practice while keeping its guarantees.

## Negative cycles

If a cycle has negative total weight, going around it again always shortens the path, so shortest paths are undefined. Bellman-Ford detects this: if any arc can still be relaxed after $n - 1$ rounds, a negative cycle is reachable from the source. Following predecessor pointers from that arc leads into the cycle.

In a constraint graph a negative cycle means the constraints are contradictory. A cycle $v_1 \to v_2 \to v_3 \to v_4 \to v_1$ with weights -6, -6, 0 and $x$ has weight $x - 12$, so the system is feasible only for $x \ge 12$. A compactor that finds such a cycle reports the constraints on it, which tells the designer exactly which spacing rules or user constraints conflict.

## Going deeper

label: Difference constraints as shortest paths
lesson:
# Difference constraints as shortest paths

Many layout and timing problems reduce to constraints of the form $x_j - x_i \le c$: minimum spacing between cell edges in compaction, register moves in retiming, and offsets in clock scheduling. A system of such constraints is a graph, and it is solved by a single shortest-path computation. This reduction is one of the most reused tricks in EDA, and it explains why compactors and retimers are fast.

## From constraints to a graph

Write each constraint $x_j - x_i \le c$ as an arc $x_i \to x_j$ of weight $c$. Add a source $x_0$ with a weight-0 arc to every variable. If the graph has no negative cycle, setting $x_k = d(x_0, x_k)$, the shortest distance from the source, satisfies every constraint, because shortest distances obey the triangle inequality $d(j) \le d(i) + c$, which is exactly $x_j - x_i \le c$.

For $x_1 - x_2 \le 3$, $x_3 - x_1 \le -2$, $x_2 - x_3 \le 6$, the arcs are $x_2 \to x_1$ (3), $x_1 \to x_3$ (-2), $x_3 \to x_2$ (6). From the source every distance is at most 0, and $x_3 = -2$. Adding a constant to every variable gives another solution, since only differences are constrained.

## Compaction by longest paths

Layout compaction uses the mirror form. A minimum-spacing rule says cell $b$'s left edge is at least cell $a$'s left edge plus $a$'s width plus a gap: $x_b \ge x_a + w_a + g$. These are arcs $a \to b$ with weight $w_a + g$, and the smallest legal positions are **longest**-path distances from the left boundary. Because left-to-right constraints form a DAG, one topological pass solves it.

Cells of widths 1, 3, 5 with constraints cell 1 before cell 2 (gap 2), cell 1 before cell 3 (gap 1), cell 2 before cell 3 (gap 0) give $x_1 = 0$, $x_2 = 3$, $x_3 = \max(0 + 1 + 1, 3 + 3 + 0) = 6$, and the row width is $6 + 5 = 11$. The longest path through the constraint graph is the critical chain that sets the width.

## Bounds and feasibility

The shortest-path distance from $x_i$ to $x_j$ is the tightest upper bound the system places on $x_j - x_i$: chaining constraints along any path from $x_i$ to $x_j$ bounds the difference by the path's weight, and the shortest-path potentials attain it. So asking how far apart two variables can be is a single-source shortest-path query.

The system is infeasible exactly when the graph has a negative cycle, which Bellman-Ford detects. In compaction that means the spacing rules cannot all be met at once, typically because of a user constraint that fixes a cell too close to another. Retiming (Leiserson and Saxe) uses the same machinery: register counts on arcs must stay non-negative, which gives difference constraints on the retiming labels, and a clock-period target adds more.

## Going deeper

Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, "Introduction to Algorithms" (4th ed., 2022), section 22.4; Leiserson and Saxe, "Retiming synchronous circuitry" (Algorithmica, 1991).

label: A* search
lesson:
# A* search

A* is Dijkstra's algorithm with a sense of direction. It orders the search by the cost so far plus an estimate of the cost to go, so a router expands vertices toward the target instead of in every direction. With an admissible estimate such as Manhattan distance on a unit-cost grid it still finds a shortest path. Every modern detailed router uses A* or a variant of it in its maze search.

## Priority f = g + h

A* keeps the cost from the source, $g(v)$, as Dijkstra does, and adds a heuristic $h(v)$ estimating the remaining cost to the target. It expands the open vertex with the smallest $f(v) = g(v) + h(v)$. On a grid with unit step cost, the Manhattan distance $h(v) = |x_v - x_t| + |y_v - y_t|$ is the natural heuristic: no route can be shorter.

A vertex at $(3, 3)$ reached with $g = 10$, routing to a target at $(7, 8)$, has $h = 4 + 5 = 9$ and $f = 19$. With $h = 0$ everywhere, A* is exactly Dijkstra. With a perfect heuristic, it expands only vertices on a shortest path.

## Which vertex is expanded next

A* expands the smallest $f$, not the smallest $g$. A vertex near the source with small $g$ but far from the target may wait, while a vertex with larger $g$ that is close to the target goes first. In an open list holding $(3, 2)$ with $g = 3$ and $(6, 12)$ with $g = 18$, routing to $(8, 14)$, the first has $f = 3 + 17 = 20$ and the second $f = 18 + 4 = 22$, so $(3, 2)$ is expanded first.

Ties on $f$ are common on grids, and breaking them toward larger $g$ (deeper vertices, closer to the target) sharply reduces expansions. The number of expansions, not the path length, is A*'s runtime, so tie-breaking and heuristic quality are the main levers a router designer has.

## Admissibility and weighted A*

A heuristic is **admissible** if it never overestimates the true remaining cost; then A* returns an optimal path. It is **consistent** if $h(u) \le c(u,v) + h(v)$ for every edge; then no vertex needs to be expanded twice. Manhattan distance is both on a unit-cost grid. If via costs or congestion raise edge costs above 1, it stays admissible; if some edges cost less than 1, it can overestimate and lose optimality.

Weighted A* uses $f = g + w h$ with $w > 1$. It expands far fewer vertices and returns a path of cost at most $w$ times the optimum when $h$ is admissible. A weighted search with $w = 2$ that returns cost 29 proves the optimum is at least 14.5. Routers trade this bounded suboptimality for speed in early iterations and tighten $w$ later.

## Going deeper

Hart, Nilsson and Raphael, "A formal basis for the heuristic determination of minimum cost paths" (IEEE Trans. SSC, 1968); the TritonRoute papers on its A*-based detailed router.

label: The cut size of a partition
lesson:
# The cut size of a partition

Partitioning splits a netlist into blocks so that few nets cross between them. It drives floorplanning, min-cut placement, multi-FPGA mapping, parallel simulation and the clustering steps inside modern placers. The objective is the cut: how many nets, or how much net weight, spans more than one block. Computing it exactly, and knowing which of its variants a tool optimizes, is the starting point for every partitioning algorithm.

## Cut nets in a bipartition

A bipartition assigns each cell to side $A$ or side $B$. A net is **cut** if it has pins on both sides. The cut size is the number of cut nets: a net counts once however many of its pins cross. For nets $n_1 = \{c_1, c_6\}$, $n_2 = \{c_2, c_3, c_5\}$, $n_3 = \{c_1, c_5\}$ and the partition $A = \{c_2, c_5\}$, $B = \{c_1, c_3, c_6\}$, net $n_1$ lies entirely in $B$, while $n_2$ and $n_3$ are cut, giving a cut size of 2.

Checking a net needs only the side of its first pin and whether any other pin differs, so the whole cut costs one pass over the pins, $O(P)$. Because each cut net becomes at least one wire crossing the block boundary, the cut is a proxy for inter-block wiring and for pins needed on each block.

## Weighted cuts

Nets carry weights when they are not equally important: a bus bit, a timing-critical net, or a coarse net standing for several merged nets. The weighted cut is $\sum_{e \text{ cut}} w(e)$. With weights 2, 4 and 3 on three cut nets and an uncut net of weight 5, the weighted cut is $2 + 4 + 3 = 9$.

Weights are also how multilevel partitioners stay exact: when coarsening merges two nets with identical pin sets, it keeps one net with the summed weight, so the coarse cut equals the fine cut of any projected partition. Timing-driven partitioning raises weights on critical nets so the optimizer avoids cutting them, at the price of cutting more of the others.

## Cut metrics for k-way partitions

With $k > 2$ blocks a net can touch several blocks, and two metrics differ. The **cut-net** metric counts each net touching more than one block once. The **connectivity** metric, $\sum_e (\lambda_e - 1)$ where $\lambda_e$ is the number of blocks net $e$ touches, charges a net spanning three blocks twice.

Connectivity models reality better: a net spread over three blocks needs wires into at least two other blocks, and in parallel computing it measures communication volume. Over the same 3-way partition, a design might have 6 cut nets but a connectivity cost of 8 because two nets touch all three blocks. Tools such as KaHyPar and PaToH optimize connectivity; hMETIS supports both, and the sum-of-external-degrees metric is a third variant. A designer must check which one a tool reports before comparing numbers.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design: From Graph Partitioning to Timing Closure" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 2; Schlag et al., "High-quality hypergraph partitioning" (ACM Journal of Experimental Algorithmics), for the connectivity metric in KaHyPar.

label: How net models distort cut size
prereqs: The cut size of a partition
Clique and star models of a net
lesson:
# How net models distort cut size

Graph partitioners and spectral methods work on ordinary graphs, so they replace each net by a clique or star. But the hypergraph cut charges a split net exactly once, while a clique charges it according to how its pins are split. Understanding that distortion explains why hypergraph partitioners beat graph partitioners on netlists, and how to weight cliques so the damage is small.

## Counting crossing clique edges

Model a $k$-pin net as a clique. If a partition puts $m$ of its pins on side $A$ and $k - m$ on side $B$, every pin on $A$ is joined to every pin on $B$, so $m(k - m)$ clique edges cross. The hyperedge itself is simply cut, cost 1.

For an 8-pin net split 4 and 4, 16 clique edges cross; split 1 and 7, only 7 cross. So a graph partitioner with unit clique edges would much rather split off one pin than split the net in half, even though both cost the same one cut net. The crossing count is maximized by the most even split, $\lfloor k/2 \rfloor \lceil k/2 \rceil$.

## Weighting to reduce the distortion

Weighting clique edges by $1/(k-1)$ makes the cost of splitting off a single pin exactly 1: $1 \cdot (k-1) / (k-1) = 1$. But an even split still costs more. A 4-pin net split 2 and 2 costs $4/3 \approx 1.33$; a 16-pin net split 8 and 8 costs $64/15 \approx 4.27$. The general cost $m(k-m)/(k-1)$ ranges from 1 up to about $k/4$.

No choice of edge weight can fix this, because the hyperedge cost is constant across splits while the clique cost depends on $m$. Weighting only rescales the curve. So graph models are always biased toward pulling large nets apart unevenly, and toward keeping them whole less strongly than the true objective does.

## Graph cut versus hypergraph cut

Over a whole netlist, the weighted graph cut is $\sum_e m_e(k_e - m_e)/(k_e - 1)$, which is at least the number of cut nets, with equality when every cut net has a single pin on one side. For a partition with 5 cut nets the graph cut might be 5.33, and a different partition with the same 5 cut nets could score higher or lower, so the two objectives can rank partitions differently.

This is the practical reason hMETIS, KaHyPar and PaToH keep nets as hyperedges: on circuit benchmarks they find substantially smaller cuts than graph partitioners applied to clique expansions. Graph models remain useful where the objective is itself a graph quantity, such as quadratic wirelength in placement, and in spectral methods, which need a Laplacian.

## Going deeper

label: Balance constraints on a bipartition
prereqs: The cut size of a partition
lesson:
# Balance constraints on a bipartition

Without a balance constraint, the best partition is trivial: put everything on one side and cut nothing. Every useful partitioning problem therefore bounds the size of each block. How the bound is stated, how a move is checked against it, and how large the resulting search space is are the practical details a partitioner designer must get right.

## The tolerance window

Let $A$ be the total cell area. A bipartition with imbalance tolerance $\epsilon$ requires each side's area $a_i$ to satisfy

$$(1 - \epsilon)\frac{A}{2} \le a_i \le (1 + \epsilon)\frac{A}{2}.$$

With $A = 286$ and $\epsilon = 0.2$, each side must hold between 114.4 and 171.6. Some tools state the bound only as an upper limit $a_i \le (1 + \epsilon) A / k$ for $k$ blocks, which implies a lower limit for bisection. Others count cells rather than area; for real netlists, with cells from tiny inverters to large flip-flops and macros, area is the meaningful measure.

## Checking a move

A move of a cell of area $s$ from side $A$ to side $B$ changes the side areas to $a_A - s$ and $a_B + s$. It is legal only if both remain inside the window. Large cells are therefore harder to move: with sides holding 35 and 32 and a window from 26.8 to 40.2, a cell of area 10 cannot move from $A$ to $B$ (B would reach 42), while a cell of area 3 can.

FM checks this for every candidate move and skips the best-gain cell when it is illegal. A tolerance that is too tight blocks many good moves and traps the search; one that is too loose produces lopsided blocks that hurt the next stage. That is why tolerances of a few percent are typical, with fixed macros handled before partitioning.

## Why exhaustive search is hopeless

For $n$ unit-area cells with $n$ even, the number of exact bisections into two unlabelled halves is $\binom{n}{n/2}/2$. For 8 cells that is 35; for 20 cells it is 92,378; for 100 cells it is about $5 \times 10^{28}$. By Stirling's formula the count grows like $2^n/\sqrt{n}$.

Minimum bisection is NP-hard, even for graphs, so no algorithm is known that avoids this growth in the worst case. Practical partitioners use local search (KL, FM) refined inside a multilevel hierarchy, and they are judged empirically on benchmark suites. Exact methods such as branch and bound or integer programming are limited to small instances, where they serve as references for testing heuristics.

## Going deeper

Garey and Johnson, "Computers and Intractability" (1979), on graph bisection; Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design: From Graph Partitioning to Timing Closure" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 2.

label: Kernighan-Lin swap gain
prereqs: The cut size of a partition
lesson:
# Kernighan-Lin swap gain

The Kernighan-Lin algorithm of 1970 was the first effective partitioning heuristic, and its gain formula is the template for every move-based partitioner since. KL improves a balanced bisection of a weighted graph by swapping pairs of vertices, choosing each swap by how much it reduces the cut. Computing those gains exactly, including the correction for an edge between the swapped pair, is the core skill.

## External and internal cost

For a vertex $v$ in a bisection, let $E(v)$ be the total weight of its edges to the other side and $I(v)$ the total weight of its edges to its own side. Define $D(v) = E(v) - I(v)$. Moving $v$ alone to the other side would reduce the cut by exactly $D(v)$: its external edges become internal and its internal edges become external.

If $v_6$ has edges of weight 5 and 1 to the other side and edges of weight 2 and 4 to its own side, then $E = 6$, $I = 6$ and $D = 0$: moving it alone would not change the cut. A positive $D$ marks a vertex that is pulled toward the other side.

## The swap gain

KL keeps exact balance by swapping a vertex $a$ from side $A$ with a vertex $b$ from side $B$. The gain is

$$g(a, b) = D(a) + D(b) - 2c(a, b),$$

where $c(a, b)$ is the weight of the edge between them (0 if none). The correction appears because $D(a)$ and $D(b)$ each count the edge $a$-$b$ as external and therefore as removed from the cut, but after the swap the two vertices are again on opposite sides, so the edge stays cut. With $D(a) = 3$, $D(b) = 2$ and $c(a,b) = 2$, the gain is $3 + 2 - 4 = 1$.

## A KL pass

A pass repeatedly picks the unlocked pair with the largest gain, tentatively swaps it, locks both vertices and updates the $D$ values of the others: for a vertex $x$ on $a$'s former side, $D(x)$ increases by $2c(x, a) - 2c(x, b)$, and symmetrically. After $n/2$ swaps the sides have fully exchanged, so KL keeps the prefix of swaps with the largest cumulative gain and undoes the rest.

The best single gain is often negative, and the pass still proceeds, because later swaps may recover more. Finding the best pair naively costs $O(n^2)$ per swap and $O(n^3)$ per pass, which limited KL to small graphs. Its other limits, unit-size vertices, exact balance and graph edges rather than nets, are what Fiduccia and Mattheyses removed.

## Going deeper

Kernighan and Lin, "An efficient heuristic procedure for partitioning graphs" (Bell System Technical Journal, 1970); Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design: From Graph Partitioning to Timing Closure" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 2.

label: Fiduccia-Mattheyses cell gain
prereqs: The cut size of a partition
lesson:
# Fiduccia-Mattheyses cell gain

The Fiduccia-Mattheyses algorithm moves one cell at a time on the hypergraph itself, under a balance tolerance. Its gain is defined directly on nets: how many cut nets a move would uncut, minus how many uncut nets it would cut. This per-net view is what makes FM handle real netlists and, with the bucket structure, run in linear time per pass.

## Nets that a move uncuts

Let cell $c$ sit on its from-side $F$. A net containing $c$ becomes uncut by the move exactly when $c$ is the only pin of that net on $F$: all its other pins are already on the to-side $T$, and moving $c$ brings the whole net together. The number of such nets is $FS(c)$.

For nets $n_2 = \{c_1, c_3, c_4, c_5\}$ with only $c_3$ on side $B$, moving $c_3$ to $A$ uncuts $n_2$, so $n_2$ counts toward $FS(c_3)$. A net where $c$ shares its side with another pin does not count, because after the move that other pin still holds the net across the cut.

## Nets that a move cuts, and the gain

A net containing $c$ becomes cut by the move exactly when all of its pins are on $F$, including $c$: the move leaves $c$ alone on $T$. The number of such nets is $TE(c)$. The FM gain is

$$g(c) = FS(c) - TE(c),$$

the decrease in the cut. Every other net of $c$ is cut both before and after, so it does not change the gain. A cell with $FS = 1$ and $TE = 0$ has gain 1; a cell sitting in the middle of two uncut nets has $FS = 0$, $TE = 2$ and gain -2. Gains are integers between $-\deg(c)$ and $\deg(c)$ for unit-weight nets, and with weights each count becomes a sum of net weights.

## Choosing among cells

FM moves the free cell with the largest gain whose move keeps balance. Ignoring balance, the best cell in a small partition is found by evaluating $FS - TE$ for each cell; for example gains 2, 1, -1, -1, 0, 0, 1, 2 give a maximum of 2, shared by two cells. Ties are frequent, so the tie-breaking rule matters.

Computing all gains from scratch costs $O(P)$, one look at every pin. FM's insight is that after a move only cells on a few nets change gain, so gains are maintained incrementally in buckets rather than recomputed. The gain is also local: it sees only the next move, so a sequence of individually poor moves can be needed to escape a local minimum, which FM handles by continuing the pass and keeping the best prefix.

## Going deeper

Fiduccia and Mattheyses, "A linear-time heuristic for improving network partitions" (Proc. Design Automation Conference, 1982); Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design: From Graph Partitioning to Timing Closure" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 2.

label: Gain buckets and incremental gain updates
lesson:
# Gain buckets and incremental gain updates

What makes FM linear per pass is not the gain formula but its data structure: an array of buckets indexed by gain, each a doubly linked list of cells, with a pointer to the highest non-empty bucket. Combined with update rules that touch only a few nets after each move, it gives constant-time selection and update. An engine designer must know its size, how updates propagate, and where it breaks down.

## Sizing the bucket array

For unit-weight nets, a cell of degree $p$ has gain between $-p$ and $p$. So each side's bucket array needs $2p_{\max} + 1$ buckets, where $p_{\max}$ is the largest cell degree in the netlist. With degrees 3, 4, 3, 4, 2, 2, 4, $p_{\max} = 4$ and each array has 9 buckets, for gains -4 through 4.

Each bucket holds the free cells with that gain in a doubly linked list, and an index into the array tracks the maximum non-empty bucket. Selecting the best cell is reading that bucket; when it empties, the pointer moves down. With weighted nets the gain range becomes the largest weighted degree, which can be huge; tools then quantize weights or switch to a heap, losing strict linear time.

## Updating gains after a move

When cell $c$ moves from $F$ to $T$, only nets of $c$ can change any gain, and only when they are **critical**: 0 or 1 pins on $T$ before the move, or 0 or 1 pins on $F$ after it. Before the move: if $T$ held 0 pins, the net was uncut and sat in the $TE$ count of every other cell on it, so each free cell on the net gains 1; if $T$ held exactly 1 pin, that cell loses the net from its $FS$, so its gain drops by 1. After the move: if $F$ holds 0 pins, every free cell on the net loses 1; if $F$ holds exactly 1 pin, that cell gains 1.

The safe way to check an update rule is recomputation: compute every cell's $FS - TE$ on the old and new partitions and compare. For a cell whose only shared net with $c$ goes from having one pin on its side to two, the gain changes; for a cell sharing only non-critical nets, it does not.

## Why updates touch few cells

Each update is a constant-time unlink and relink between buckets. A net's state changes only a bounded number of times per pass once its pins are locked, so the total update work over a pass is $O(P)$. In practice, after one move only a handful of cells change gain: those on the moved cell's critical nets.

Two engineering consequences follow. First, the order cells are inserted into a bucket (LIFO or FIFO) breaks ties and measurably changes results; LIFO tends to keep moving cells near recent moves, which helps. Second, the incremental bookkeeping is easy to get wrong in edge cases (nets with duplicate pins, nets entirely of locked cells), so engines verify the incrementally maintained cut against a full recount in testing.

## Going deeper

Fiduccia and Mattheyses, "A linear-time heuristic for improving network partitions" (Proc. DAC, 1982); Hagen, Huang and Kahng, "On implementation choices for iterative improvement partitioning algorithms" (IEEE TCAD, 1997).

label: The Fiduccia-Mattheyses algorithm
prereqs: Gain buckets and incremental gain updates
lesson:
# The Fiduccia-Mattheyses algorithm

The Fiduccia-Mattheyses algorithm is the local-search engine at the heart of almost every netlist partitioner, from flat bipartitioning to the refinement step of hMETIS and KaHyPar. It runs passes of single-cell moves under a balance tolerance, locks each moved cell, and commits the best prefix of each pass. Understanding the pass structure is what lets a designer predict its behaviour and its limits.

## One pass of tentative moves

At the start of a pass all cells are free and their gains are in the buckets. The pass repeatedly picks the free cell with the highest gain whose move keeps balance, moves it, **locks** it so it cannot move again in this pass, updates its neighbours' gains, and records the gain. The pass ends when no free cell can move.

Locking guarantees termination and bounds a pass to at most $n$ moves. Moves are tentative: the pass may make many moves with zero or negative gain, because later moves may pay them back. The recorded gain sequence, for example $0, 2, 3, -2, 0, -2, -2$, is the raw material for the commit decision.

## Committing the best prefix

After the pass, FM computes cumulative gains $G_j = g_1 + \dots + g_j$ and keeps the prefix with the largest $G_j$, undoing every later move. For gains $0, 2, 3, -2, 0, -2, -2$ the cumulative gains are $0, 2, 5, 3, 3, 1, -1$, so the best prefix is the first three moves. Starting from a cut of 15, the committed cut is $15 - 5 = 10$.

Two wrong rules are tempting. Stopping at the first negative gain misses recoveries later in the pass. Keeping all moves can end worse than the start, here at 16. If the best cumulative gain is 0 (the empty prefix), the pass made no progress and the algorithm stops; otherwise a new pass starts from the committed partition.

## Strengths and limits

With gain buckets, a pass runs in $O(P)$ time, and only a few passes are usually needed, so FM is fast enough to run millions of times inside larger flows. It handles hyperedges and cell areas directly, which KL could not.

Its weakness is locality. Moving one cell of a tightly connected cluster rarely has positive gain, so FM seldom relocates a whole cluster, and on large netlists it converges to poor local minima that depend on the starting partition. Remedies are many random starts (expensive), smarter tie-breaking, lookahead gains (Krishnamurthy's higher-level gains), and above all the multilevel scheme, which runs FM on coarsened netlists where one move relocates a cluster.

## Going deeper

Fiduccia and Mattheyses (Proc. DAC, 1982); Krishnamurthy, "An improved min-cut algorithm for partitioning VLSI networks" (IEEE Trans. Computers, 1984); Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design: From Graph Partitioning to Timing Closure" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 2.

label: Coarsening by heavy-edge matching
prereqs: Clique and star models of a net
lesson:
# Coarsening by heavy-edge matching

Multilevel partitioners shrink the netlist level by level, contracting groups of strongly connected cells into single vertices. The simplest and most widely used grouping is a matching: pair up adjacent vertices and contract each pair. Which pairs are chosen decides how much connection weight disappears inside clusters, and therefore how good the coarse problem is.

## Greedy heavy-edge matching

Visit the vertices in some order, often random. When the current vertex is unmatched, match it with the unmatched neighbour joined by the heaviest edge; if no unmatched neighbour remains, leave it single. The result is a matching, a set of disjoint pairs, found in one pass over the edges.

With edges $v_1$-$v_2$ (9), $v_1$-$v_6$ (6), $v_3$-$v_5$ (6), $v_2$-$v_5$ (6), visited in the order $v_6, v_3, v_5, v_1, v_2$: $v_6$ matches $v_1$ (its only neighbour), $v_3$ matches $v_5$, then $v_5$ and $v_1$ are already matched, and $v_2$ finds no unmatched neighbour. The heaviest edge $v_1$-$v_2$ was missed because $v_6$ took $v_1$ first, which shows how the visit order matters.

## Contracting matched pairs

Each matched pair becomes one coarse vertex whose weight is the sum of the two areas. Edges between two coarse vertices merge, with weights added. The coarse graph has $n - |M|$ vertices for a matching of $|M|$ pairs; a matching that pairs most vertices roughly halves the size per level.

With 8 vertices and 2 matched pairs, the coarse graph has 6 vertices, a weak reduction. Real coarseners therefore try to match as many vertices as possible, and hypergraph coarseners often use clustering schemes (each vertex joins its best neighbouring cluster) that shrink faster than strict matchings. Vertex-weight caps keep any cluster from growing so large that balance becomes impossible.

## Why heavy edges

Any edge inside a coarse vertex can never be cut by a partition of the coarse graph. The weight left exposed is the original total minus the matched weight. If the total edge weight is 48 and the matching hides 24, any coarse partition can cut at most 24.

Heavy-edge matching greedily maximizes the hidden weight, which lowers the cut available at the coarse level and keeps strongly connected pairs together, as a good fine partition would. For hypergraphs the analogue is a rating function, such as the sum over shared nets of $w(e)/(|e| - 1)$, which favours pairs sharing many small nets. Good coarsening is what lets the coarse solution be close to a good fine solution, so most quality differences between multilevel tools come from it.

## Going deeper

Karypis and Kumar, "A fast and high quality multilevel scheme for partitioning irregular graphs" (SIAM J. Scientific Computing, 1998); Karypis, Aggarwal, Kumar and Shekhar, "Multilevel hypergraph partitioning: applications in VLSI domain" (IEEE TVLSI, 1999).

problems.q: A weighted graph has edges v1-v3 (4), v1-v5 (1), v2-v4 (9), v2-v5 (1), v3-v5 (8), v4-v6 (4), v5-v6 (1). Heavy-edge matching visits vertices in the order v4, v6, v5, v3, v2, v1; an unmatched vertex is matched to its unmatched neighbour with the heaviest edge (ties go to the smaller number), or stays single if none is left. Which vertex is v4 matched with? Answer with its number.
